title: Brunei and the Philippines
hook: Muslim sultanates of Borneo and Mindanao

segments.voice: Yesterday, Indonesia, the largest Muslim country, and one faith speaking in many island languages. Did you get to say terima kasih to anyone? Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

A street sign in Brunei, on the island of Borneo. The name of the road is written twice. Once in Latin letters, the way Malay is usually written today. And once above it, in flowing Arabic letters. Same words, same language, two alphabets. That second script, Jawi, is Malay written in the letters of the Qur'an, and it is a small, daily clue to a bigger story. North and east of Borneo, across the sea, on the southern islands of the Philippines, there are clues like it. Today: Brunei and the Philippines.
screen: `A STREET SIGN IN BRUNEI.` → `ONE NAME, TWO ALPHABETS.` → `JAWI: MALAY IN ARABIC LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The trade winds that carried merchants to Malacca also carried them along the coasts of Borneo and up into the southern Philippine islands. Where trading towns took up Islam, local rulers often took a new title: sultan. On Borneo, the Sultanate of Brunei grew into a sea power along the coast, and it is still ruled by a sultan today, with Islam at the heart of public life and Jawi on its signs. Further north, on the islands of Sulu and Mindanao, the Sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao rose and ruled the seas and rivers around them. Their Muslim peoples, the Tausug, the Maguindanao, the Maranao and others, are often called together the Moro. When Spain later took the northern islands, the southern sultanates resisted, and that history of struggle over land and self-rule runs long and hard, into modern times. Today much of the Muslim south forms the Bangsamoro autonomous region, within the Philippines. And there are stories. Around Lake Lanao, the Maranao people keep the Darangen, a long epic sung by performers, full of heroes, journeys, love and the old kingdom of Bembaran. It was sung at weddings and gatherings, holding up a people's memory of who they are. The Qur'an has a line about peoples and their differences: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Sultans, seas, an epic by a lake. The sultanates of the islands.
screen: `TRADE WINDS TO BORNEO AND THE ISLANDS.` · `BRUNEI: A SULTAN STILL REIGNS.` · `SULU, MAGUINDANAO, THE MORO.` · `THE DARANGEN BY LAKE LANAO.` · then, large: `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one of their stories, starting with the shape of one. Settle, and breathe. An epic is a people remembering out loud. Think of one story your own family or town keeps telling: a journey, a hero, a loss, a wedding that went wrong. Run it through your mind slowly, the way a singer would. Then hold it next to the Darangen, sung by a lake far away. Different heroes, the same human need to remember. If you pray, you can ask for the good of the people of those islands. The bell holds the time.
Brunei and the Philippines. Sultanates of Borneo, Sulu and Mindanao, where Islam came by sea and sultans ruled the waters. Today's word.
Your line: the sultanates of the islands. Today, look up one Moro or Bruneian story, a scene from the Darangen or a tale from Sulu, and read it through. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: In Brunei, Islam shapes public life and Malay is written in both Latin letters and Jawi; Muslims of the southern Philippines keep their own languages, sung epics such as the Darangen, and traditions from the old sultanates.
